Private Artemyev stood as still as stone. The wooden floor creaked beneath their feet.

Yazov raised his head to the rafters. "I would not be proud of shooting rats, Private. I advise you to keep your attention on duty." He raised an eyebrow. "Now, please light this garbage on fire."[Change Later]

options.name: Passion alone could not save them.

title: Last Stand of Madness
desc:
An RPG soared through the sky and exploded in a fireball against Taboritsky's grand palace. The fine marble and gold inlays were ruined from three days of heavy gunfire. The Black League fired from all directions, unleashing a hailstorm of brass and the mighty thunder of cannons. The defenders knelt in trenches, their cover whittling away, praying that God would intervene and save the Holy Regent.

The League's soldiers saw an opening, and squads flooded the palace grounds. Fervent guards stood their ground, some felled by a single bullet, others taking a few more. Afterwards, a handful of attackers swore they saw a man with ragged hair and bloodshot eyes stand up even after a round pierced his lung.

The agonizing slog of claiming the compound section by section took the rest of the afternoon. Every corridor, every room, every hall was trapped, every corner held an ambush. When Taboritsky's men ran out of ammunition, they turned to knives and blood streaked fists.

By the end of the day, the League claimed five hundred and eighty six scalps. The few who were captured refused to repent their allegiance. They showed no regret, and died believing in their own righteousness. But of the many, many corpses, none belonged to Taboritsky. The League's men double-checked, triple-checked, and, with the guiding hand of the Interrogation Cadres, quadruple checked. Their conclusion remained the same: Regent Taboritsky had escaped.

The League's leadership ground its teeth and wailed its anger. Orders were given, subordinates punished. But they could not overawe the joy in the hearts of soldiers and civilians alike as the disgraceful flag of the Holy Russian Empire lowered from its pole. Taboritsky's twisted vision for Russia was grounded into dust, here, forever.

options.name: Sic Semper Tyrannis.

title: Memorandum No. 45,862
desc:
From the desk of Glacoverk Dimitry Timofeyevich Yazov, leader of our nation and follower of our founder Karbyshev:

I congratulate all of you Russians who have participated in this great pacification operation of the tyrannical dictator Ivan Serov. As many of you know, and as much as that mentally ill troglodyte has tried to establish, Ordosocialism is dead.

His ideals of Fascist Communism is fundamentally a broken system. Many years ago, when the Black League broke from the yolk of the West Siberian Socialist Republic, Karbyshev and now I made a promise to never submit to the opiates of Communism and Bukharanist thought. That the ideals of Marx, Lenin, and all other socialist revolutionaries have done nothing to truly help people. They have led the Russian people astray.

Was it not that Lenin was sent on a train from Switzerland to the old Monarchy due to the German menace? And was it not that Marx and Engels were Germans? Clearly these two snakes have had the ability to run rampant throughout all of Russia and Ordosocialism is the final binding of Communism with their Germanic origin. I, personally, am happy that we have aborted this way of thought before it festered within our great nation long enough.

The only saving grace that this unredeemable man has accomplished within his borders of Western Russia was his industrial programs. He has turned the nation into a factory, albeit one of fear and hate. We shall begin using these facilities to create better weapons of war in order to fully blot out the German cloud.

Thank you.

options.name: Signed, Dmitry Yazov.

title: Recursive Failures
desc:
Yazov looked at the plethora of military reports on his desk, this was it. Victory in Western Russia had been achieved, the resilient and loyal soldiers of the Black League had marched across the Urals and swiftly crushed any resistance. He put down the pile of papers, before slumping over in his chair.

The Soviet Union was gone; left shattered by the Germanic marauders in the First Trial. The deceitful, incompetent ways of Bukharin cascading Russa into chaos. Yazov thought of his time fighting on the Eastern Front, forced to retreat beyond the A-A line, humiliated by the Union's failures. Oh, the young Soviet Union was his homeland, one he was supposed to defend and feel a sense of patriotism for, but seeing Bukharin's failures first hand, it shed a light on its shortcomings. In what was the tragedy of what was the fall of the U.S.S.R, something could be salvaged: information. If the Black League ever needed to survive, it needed the knowledge of how to avoid the faults of the Union.

But Yazov knew that knowledge was a fickle thing, some people were stubborn enough to deliberately copy the mistakes of the past, and Bukharina was no exception. She was like a caricature of her father, showing the worst parts of him. All this talk of "Marxist dialectics", "the proletariat", but how does this serve the Russian people beyond pseudo-intellectual discussion? The Soviet Union was gone, and Bukharina's death cemented it.

options.name: The hydra pervading Russia has been slayed.

title: MEMORANDUM 93: Communist Ideology
desc:
From the desk of Glavkoverkh Dmitry Timofeyevich Yazov, leader of our nation and follower of our founder Dmitry Karbyshev:

I write having just been informed of the unconditional surrender of the treacherous communist government of Mikhail Suslov. I would like to take this opportunity to reflect on communism and its effects on our nation.

I was once a communist. Communism and its proponents have long held admirable goals for Russia. It saved us from complete destruction following the civil war, and brought some measure of economic strength to our nation. I grew up in Bukharin’s Russia, and I joined Bukharin’s Red Army in 1941 to fight the Teutonic menace. Later, I joined the Revolutionary Front and took up arms once again in the West Russian War. Throughout this time, I believed in communism, and its vision of a truly strong and prosperous Russia.

However, I need not remind anyone that both Red Armies I fought in ultimately lost, undermined by petty squabbling and weak idealism of their political leadership. This is where the lofty ideals of Lenin and Bukharin fall apart. They cannot survive the siege that we, the Russian nation, find ourselves under. The Germanic horde cannot be fought with equality, it cannot be fought with dialectics, it cannot even be fought with prosperity. No, the Teutons can only be fought with steel. Violence alone is our defense against the arsenal the Teutons bring against them, of which communism is in fact a component. Need I remind you where Marx, the inventor of this Germanic corruption of the Russian nation, comes from? Need I remind you that Lenin himself was sent here by the Teutons to undermine us in the Great War?

Communism is not a defense for the Russian nation, nay, it is yet another sword pointed by the Teutons at our heart.

options.name: Signed, Dmitry Yazov.

title: Report BP-DPL-WQ8
desc:
Identifier: BP-DPL-WQ8

Composer: BLP-NV-3

Classification: 2A+

Concerning: Salvage of People's Commissariat of Science

Background: Following capitulation of Soviet Federation, Scientific Cadre 112685 ordered to amass, investigate, and identify useful research and 'blue sky' technologies developed by the People's Commissariat of Science. Interrogation Cadre 356707 ordered to interrogate surviving Federation personnel to accomplish this objective.

Findings: Ninety-five percent of technologies recorded in People's Commissariat archives classified by 112685 as Class Zero (Not Recommended for Further Inquiry). Further three percent classified as Class One (Potential Civilian Applications) and two percent classified as Class Two (Potential Military Applications). Personnel note that scientific research in the Federation was driven by political concerns and as a method of personal aggrandisement rather than potential use cases. Additionally, personnel note possible logistics concerns with technologies in Class Two category, as many will require heavy industrial investment to be produced at a significant scale.

One item noted as Class Three (Immediate Military Applications). Project CHEREPAKHA is a long distance, supersonic bomber. Existing data and blueprints indicate measurable superiority over current Black League air assets in both speed, resilience, and air power. Further information in Appendix A-74-SSI (attached).

One item noted as Class Four (Immediate and Significant Military Applications). Project CHERENKOV is a re-engineered medium tank design involving a number of design superiorities including mobility over rough terrain, decreased reload time, and armor plating designed to minimize the effects of radiation exposure to crew. Recommend immediate production of test models and exercises using CHERENKOV models within twelve months.

options.name: [Change Later]"Recommendations accepted."[Change Later]

title: [Change Later]"MEMORANDUM 884: Monarchist Collaborationism"[Change Later]
desc:
[Change Later]"Comrade soldiers! We celebrate together as we rip the collaborationist parasite from our lands. The Sovereignty of Western Russia is no more. Our victory is evidence of our superiority and our righteousness. Indeed, it is the only evidence a soldier needs.

It has not escaped the soldiers who conquered the Tsar's palace that he lived in splendor while his people scraped in poverty. Monarchism is, by its nature, corrupt. By empowering men of weak bodies and corrupt minds for their bloodline, it ensures only that the nation is led by bandits, the vainglorious, and the self-obsessed. Comrade soldiers, there is only one bloodline which matters: the bloodline of Russia!

Monarchism is a yearning for the past. It denies, even despises the present, searching ever backwards for the image of power and respect. But we know that respect comes to those who earn it, and power comes not from symbols but from action.

Our Russia is a land of merit. Where the strong shall lead, and become stronger for it. Where strength of body, strength of mind, and strength of will define your duties, and your rewards. Our Russia is led by men of humble beginnings. The League is made up of diligent men of firm character, not those empowered by an accident of birth. Our Russia is a land of the present, neither indulging in fancies of the future nor denying the sorrows of the past. Our eyes are fixed on the here and now, upon duty, and upon the actions we must take to leave the precipice of annihilation.

We who have conquered the present have overturned those who obsess over the past. There is only today. There is only duty."[Change Later]

options.name: [Change Later]"And only in death does duty end."[Change Later]

title: The Traitor's Call
desc:
This had to work. There were no other options left for Bunyachenko. The League had beaten him time and again. They had driven his people from the Ural Mountains. They had driven them back to the Kama River, and they had driven them back until the only thing behind his men was the Reichskomissarat. At every engagement, the League had shown more fortitude and more cunning. They were like a steel blade cutting through his men in one clean sweep. But he would never back down or surrender. Not to them. Not to any man. He would save Russia from itself.

"Men," Bunyachenko began to speak as he paced before a few dozen soldiers, the last remnants of his army. "On the other side of this hill is the bulk of the League's army. They're tired from fighting us. They have had to travel over hundreds of miles of our land. And they have butchered everything in sight. They have laid waste to your villages, your cities, and your families. Your wives and and children may have even died at the hands of one of those monsters on the other side of that hill. And did they shed a tear for any of them? Did any of them show an ounce of mercy for the many they've killed? No.

"Let's show them what they deserve. They want to cleanse Russia of its filth? I agree. They want to purify Russia, so that it can stand strong once again as a mighty power? I couldn't agree more. And in our shared mission to free Russia of degeneracy, I say we start with the men in black over these fucking hills!"

He raised his rifle to the cheers of his men, all their eyes looking up to him with inspiration, young and old. Perhaps they could still do this. Perhaps they could pull victory from the jaws of defeat. Who knew? Yazov himself could be standing at the head of the army, and this charge might make it far enough to kill him, and leave the black snake leaderless as it eats itself from within. So many possibilities ran through Bunyachenko's mind as he turned, and charged over the hill. On the other side were hundreds of League soldiers waiting for them. And the moment enough of them had charged over the ridge, they opened fire and let their bullets spray into the bodies of Bunyachenko and his men.

options.name: No mercy for traitors.

title: The Negotiating Table
desc:
There must have been twenty of them. They wore black uniforms and peaked caps, each patched and repaired with scraps of the same ink colored cloth. Each of them was armed even beyond what was expected of an ROA soldier- machineguns, pistols, agglomerations of miscellaneous ammunition, knives and trunchions dangled from overful waists and bent backs. Zykov trembled whenever one grew near. He'd rather be anywhere but sitting at this dusty banquet tablel; but it was here, or a gallows.

The floor creaked as General Sakharovsky, the League's representative in these negotiations, sat down. He slid his bony hand onto the back of  Zykov's neck. "Now then, Mister President," the smirking officer said, "Let's get down to business. Your armies are decimated, and good Russians are fleeing for their lives. The League is more than happy to slaughter the surviving ROA formations in Gorky and Vologda." The General's grip tightened. "But I believe that cooler heads can prevail. I believe that, should you concede to total annexation and order the survivors of your military to stand down, the League may be inclined to commute your sentence to life imprisonment."

Zykov’s heart sank. "Gentlemen, Gentlemen," he said, desperately glancing around the room for an ally. The League's soldiers were cold, not ever glaring in anger as he pleaded. "We are civilized men here! There's no need to leave an experienced propagandist like me to rot. Surely we can work something out."

Sakhavorsky clicked his tongue. "Corporal Ivanova, could you forge the President's signature?"

One of the soldiers nodded. "Yes, sir. With enough time."

The General smiled. "Well, it seems we don't need you after all, President Aleksandrovich. It has been a pleasure."

Before Zykov could respond, two men with Titanium grips grabbed him by the shoulders and pulled him from the table. He wanted to scream, he wanted to make a desperate plea, to beg for his life. In the end, all that escaped his mouth was a terrified wail.

options.name: All ROA soldiers are hereby ordered to immediately surrender. Signed, President Meletios Aleksandrovich Zykov.

title: The Great Scam Ends
desc:
The bottom of the vodka bottle never looked more beautiful. Or perhaps it was simply the fact that Oktan couldn't see it very well, with his hand swaying this way and that, and his eyes only able to make out vague shapes swimming across his vision. He still had to finish the last bit of it, though. Couldn't very well let it go to waste. So he turned the bottle over his cup, pouring out the last of it before tossing the bottle aside and letting it shatter against the hardwood of his office. He took hold of his glass, leaned back, and shot the drink down his throat, before throwing the glass over to join the bottle as shards across the floor.

He could have lived like a king. He had been using the Germans like marionettes, and they were singing to his tune just as he'd wanted. The whole of Russia could have been his domain with their help, and he could have taken whatever he fucking wanted from whoever he fucking wanted. But no. Yazov and his band of radicals had to storm across the Urals and beat back his army. What fucking use is an army if they can't defend some god damn mountains?

Oktan looked back to his desk, eyes locked on a German Luger lying on top. He reached over and took hold of it, twirling it between his fingers lazily. Perhaps he could run away with what he could carry, and live it rich in the Caribbean or South America. Somewhere tropical. But he could hear gunshots approaching from outside. He couldn't run, not anymore; Yazov's men were far too close. He wouldn't make it ten miles. No, there was nothing he could do.

He pressed the barrel against the underside of his chin, feeling the coolness of the metal spreading across his skin. He had no illusions about some supposed afterlife; once the trigger was pulled, darkness would be Oktan's eternal companion. All of the money that he's amassed won't matter. It'll all be used to fuel Yazov's war machine. The glory of leading West Russia would be swept away to the dustbin of history. Oktan would be a footnote, and nothing more. Yes, darkness was all he had left before him. He let his finger squeeze down on the trigger as he painted the wall with his head.

options.name: The German puppet falls.

title: All is Lost
desc:
The city was burning. The air was choked with ash and smoke and embers, scraps of a dream deferred that drifted on the wind like fireflies. Private Koslov held his left arm over his face, hoping to ward the sting from his watering eyes. He failed. The young man, barely sixteen, stumbled over wood and rubble, his Kalashnikov clutched by the cold barrel.

In the distance, he could hear screaming. The invaders were growling, roaring their hate like animals. They had slipped past language into the primordial. Beneath their shouts, he could hear civilians — women — begging for mercy. Their speech was crushed under the hammerfall of gunshots.

Koslov's bowels ran cold. The stripling broke out in a sweat as he scrabbled through chalk and fallen beams, forcing himself forward on his hands and knees. He had to escape. He had to get away from this nightmare, retreat, live to fight another day -

"Help me." A phantom's moan drifted on the burning wind.  "Please... help me."

Koslov wiped the tears and smoke from his eyes. Everything around him was an indistinguishable ruin, the same pattern of broken concrete and toppled walls. Without thinking, the words slipped from his mouth. "W-where-" He cleared his throat, spitting black phlegm into the dust. "Where are you?"

A scraping sound came from his left, and Koslov saw him. He was a man, or the remnants of one. The soldier was middle aged, balding, with a curly grey beard and the patch of the Utopian salon's militia sewn onto the breast pocket of his uniform. And his legs had been crushed by a falling beam. An arm dangled by the man's side, useless.

Koslov knew what the soldier wanted before he even spoke. Mercy. A reprieve from the animals that hunted Tomsk's ruins. But the League was close, and growing closer by the second. He could feel their breath on his neck...

"I'm sorry." The boy turned as the soldier wailed in horror, and sprinted for the city's outskirts. For survival, and shame.

options.name: Pragmatism — another word for cowardice.

title: A Struggle Forgotten
desc:
The building had since been cleared of any sort of hostile presence, and been swept for mines and traps. Though Pavel still lingered, this previously being an administrative center, perhaps there could be something interesting here. Be it actually useful intelligence, or just simple curiosity, trivia and the like. He stubbed his cigarette out on the windowsill, and flicked it into the cold evening air before turning back to the dilapidated hallway he was in. Something at the far end caught his eye, though.

A records room, perhaps something worth his time could be found there? He wandered in, the room lined floor to ceiling with filing cabinets, some torn from the walls, their contents flung all about. On a large and long table in the middle of the room where the pencil pushers likely did their tiresome work, sat a file marked in red which caught his eye. “ARREST RECORDS 1962-64” it practically screamed. He picked it up and flipped it open a few pages in.

Names, many many names. Accompanied by a brief description of their crime as well as a sentence. The document was rather thick, there could easily be over a thousand names in this record. Not to speak of other such records like this one. While idly scanning over it, something caused him to raise an eyebrow. “Valery Mikhailovich Sablin” it read “Rebellion against the state. Mutiny. Sedition. Sentence: Execution, firing squad” it stated bluntly.

With a dry laugh, and an overarm throw into a waste paper bin on the far side of the room, the document hit its mark with a dry thump. Making his way out, he struck a match and ignited another cigarette, meeting a pair of other officers who’d been lingering on the steps outside the building.

“Find anything interesting?” one of them asked disinterestedly, tobacco smoke clouding the air around them.

“Not really” Pavel replied, leaning on the doorframe. “Arrest and sentence records mostly, building's shot to shit. Would be more trouble than it's worth to get it back to working order” he continued, taking a long drag.

"might be able to recycle some materials from in there, wiring might still be good” his comrade suggested

Pavel tilted his head, considering this “I’ll get in contact with command, strip out anything useful and demolish the rest” he said with finality.

options.name: To the dustbin of history.

title: Cold Comfort
desc:
Igor had seen much in his time, born at the turn of the century and long before all the triumphs and tragedies that had ensued. He sat back in an old armchair while the fire crackled close by, leaning his head back as a feeling of nostalgia bit at him and he began to reminisce.

The first pictures to run through his mind were of the revolution which put the Bolsheviks in power. He was only a young man at the time, still living in Angarsk, so the revolution was well underway by the time news reached him. While he worked in a workshop at the time, all he had heard from friends and colleagues was of the revolution. Igor had been concerned that a new government would be no better than the old one.

The turmoil didn’t end there; various names vied for power, with Bukharin eventually coming out on top after Stalin's death. But that wasn’t the end of it. The Great Patriotic War would prove trying for everyone. Igor was shocked when news that Moscow had fallen filtered through. He had worked long and exhausting hours in a factory, likely inducing his current arthritis and it had all been for nothing. 

After that, the union which had seemed so very invincible shattered like a stone through a glass panel. Igor felt as though a trapdoor had opened beneath him, his mind spun with uncertainty as warlords sprung up across the broken nation. When his arthritis rendered him unable to work, he thankfully had family to move in with in the face of the whirlwinds of danger racing around him.

Despite bravado about scattering the Black League, the opposite had taken place, and now the League’s troops paraded through Irkutsk. But, if the Black League had picked up the pieces of a shattered nation, perhaps they could be strong enough to one day face the Reich? One could only hope. And these days, a single hope is enough to sustain you like a log in a fire.

options.name: The cold kept at bay.

title: Broken, But Not Shattered
desc:
Tank 237, was wandering around Siberian villages for nearly the whole afternoon, tasked with advanced reconnaissance to investigate rumors of Sablinite resistance following their government's capitulation. All of the villages they passed, from farming hamlets to town hubs were vacant, not a single soul was seen.  Abandoned buildings and town squares were devoid of life, with the occasional dead farm animal being feasted upon by wolves or crows. It was uncannily quiet, with the break in silence coming from the embers of a burning barn. Eventually, the crew of 237 stopped, their fuel had begun to run out. Luckily their logistics convoy was just a short distance behind and was coming to help refuel. The tank commander, Nevsky, climbed out and pulled out one of his cigars before lighting it. The fire from the stub tickling his cheekbones with comforting albeit brief warmth. He looked around, Nevsky assumed that the population fled in the face of their advance.

The fuel truck arrived and began refilling 237’s tank. It took a while but eventually  they were good to go, that was before a loud whistle and a house next to the tank exploded. Coming from the dense tree line in front of Tank 237, a rocket was fired, which was followed by a crescendo of bullets coming from the same direction. The small Black League convoy went into disarray. Everyone expected that the Sablinite army was scattered. They were wrong, it was there, and still had some fight in it. Finally, the main turret of the tank started to return fire. It was unclear how long the battle would last, but it was clear that blood would have to be shed.

options.name: The last followers of Lenin, raging against the dying of the light.

title: We Dared to hope
desc:
It was a new morning in Bada, Pavlov, the mayor, entered the town hall like any other day. The war with the black league passed them, and the fate of Sablin's Nation is unknown. But they were sure to have some rough months, maybe years from now on. Everyone greeted Pavlov as he moved with his briefcase up the stairs. The heating and lights were cut off the grid so they had to use generators. He eventually made it to the front of his office and opened the door. He placed his briefcase next to his desk as he laid back to catch his breath before a long day of work. He looked at his desk and saw an envelope. He opened it to see in big and red colors the word, NOTICE, reading it was the black league informing him about his town being on his territory now and that all orders are to be obeyed.

He breathed a sigh of relief. At least it didn't mean he would get shot. He eventually put the envelope to his side and began working. Yet, it wouldn't last. At around noon he heard something outside. After looking outside his window he saw a truck with a jeep in front of it parking in front of the town hall. He jumped out of his chair to investigate while passing all of his worried staff. As soon as he came outside an Officer stopped him with his palm pointing towards him.

"Under the Order of the Black League, you are to follow us."

Before he could respond one of the soldiers viciously grabbed both of his hands and placed them behind his head, while the others entered to look for his staff. He was led behind the Town Hall and placed on his knees. It was freezing. The officer lit up a cigarette behind him, after the officer saw him looking at him, he looked to see if the others were back, but they weren't, he was quick to place a cigarette in his mouth and lit it up while quickly returning to his position. After around 10 minutes the building was clear. His staff were all standing with their heads to the wall. They didn't say a word. Pavlov didn't say a word.

"PREPARE!" The Officer shouted as the men loaded their rifles.

"PRESENT!" The Staff were all panicking as Pavlov's secretary began crying. Yet he didn't panic, and he didn't cry, it was over, and the only way to accept it was by accepting what was going to happen. In his last moments, he thought of the officer who allowed him one last smoke.

options.name: [Change Later]"FIRE!"[Change Later]

title: Guilty after Guilty
desc:
The war was over. Whatever was left of the Amur government was in Black League hands. Igor woke up as always, washed his face, got his uniform, and left the barracks just to see that he had the honor of guarding a tribunal of blackshirts. After being driven in a truck with his comrades they arrived in front of the courthouse.  Igor stood straight with his rifle for around an hour, it was surprisingly warm inside the courtroom of all places. For at least half an hour he had seen at least four black shirts already guilty and sentenced to be shot. One of them didn't even have time to say anything. He didn't exactly understand why the court was even in session if every defendant was sentenced to death almost instantly. Perhaps for propaganda.

Two hours passed as more blackshirts were tried, all of them guilty and sentenced to death for treason. Yet one seemed to be more aggressive than his other ilk. He was trying to push the two guards carrying him away while shouting slurs and calling everyone "Jewish pigs". The two guards eventually forced him to sit down. The judge attempted to talk only for him to shout again at each attempt. A bailiff eventually got tired, pulled out his pistol, and without hesitation pulled the trigger behind his head. His head fell flat on the table and his body simply carried away shortly after. When the next defendant came in he was visibly disturbed by the fresh blood stain that tainted the wood covered desk, continuously looking behind him to check if he was going to meet his end on the chair as well.

It eventually ended after ten painful hours and Igor was soon on the truck heading back to his apartment. It was exhausting to just stand up, but the extra rations were worth it. While Igor was sitting on his bed his partner on the bed next to him asked how his day was. Igor simply looked at her and sighed.

options.name: [Change Later]"Exhausting."[Change Later]

title: The Merchants of Death, Outsold
desc:
In an unmarked room, in an unincorporated town, on the outskirts of Magadan, two men who weren't in Russia, along with one who most certainly was, sat down to have a meeting that never happened to discuss a state that never was.

"Alexander Lazarenko, I take it? We, uh, assure you that the United States of America had nothing to do with the deranged misadventures of that madman Werbell. Rather, we seek to ensure continued diplomatic ties with-"

"-You Americans are too damn sloppy."

"Excuse me?"

"You prop up an illegal puppet state on Russian soil, and upon its inevitable destruction act as if you had no hand in it. I know your game, and I have to say you're terrible at playing it."

"I apologize, Mr. Lazarenko, but there seems to have been a misunderstanding. The CIA would not back foreign dictators and warlords, nor would it operate against its allies. We simply ask for this to be cleaned up as nothing more than a minor, inconsequential stain on the clean surface of Russo-American cordiality, and for all CIA operatives and assets in the region to be allowed to be withdrawn. Surely a reasonable government such as yours would be more than amenable to such requests?"

For a moment, there was silence. Then, the sound of something sliding on the floor.

"Mr. Lazarenko you can't be serious-"

"Leave. And do not return. Let this generosity be the last act of its kind required."[Change Later]

options.name: And all that was left was a single, bloodied cap, lying still upon the floor.

title: Where Did We Go Wrong?
desc:
The dripping of water, the bad bed quality, the horrendous smell. Shukshin and Amet-Kahn were already beginning to get used to their new cell. Two small rusty beds with the worst mattress known to mankind, a sink, and a toilet that doesn't work. They were both still in their stained suits, as they were never even given a proper prisoner uniform. They were both staring at the ceiling until Amet-Kahn broke the silence.

"Where did we go wrong?"

Shukshin turned his head.

"Did we build too little? Did we prepare too little? Did we hope too little? Did we cause this?"

Shukshin would've normally said something to make his friend feel less guilty, but he was facing the reality, that he felt the same guilt as him. The unification wars were quite literally the worst time of his life. His winning against Pokryskin brought him hope, hope that things were finally going to get better. But when more and more reports came in detailing in mass detail how the Black League was seeing victory after victory. It gave him nightmares, and it seemed that the nightmares would become real. He was about to say something but then they heard a voice.

"Amet Khan Sultan, follow us please."

They both looked up to see men dressed all in black as if he was preparing for a funeral, one was an officer, and the two behind his shoulders were soldiers. Shukshin looked scared but Amet Khan didn't show a single expression, he simply got up and exited the cell, but before he left he turned to Shukshin one last time and said.

"I'll see you soon."

Shukshin sat in his cell alone, for hours, or so he assumed was hours, he lost track of time a long time ago. He was tired, but everything in him refused to rest. As things couldn't get worse. A shiver ran down his spine as the same officer came back..

options.name: [Change Later]"Let's get this over with, ‘Mr. President’."[Change Later]

title: Almost Painless
desc:
It was over, Novosibirsk has fallen. The Black League was advancing daily as the All-Siberian Army could do little to nothing at stopping their advance. What was left was no longer about defense but of evacuating. While the soldiers were fighting, many civilians were fleeing. The Siloviki, once the most influential men in the country, were reduced to a bunch of greedy businessmen getting on whatever that could fly to escape, either to their estates abroad in Japan or America or any country that would accept their money.

A prime example would be Artem Makarov, once sitting on the Sibir board of directors now running alongside his staff toward his private jet. All around the airfield civilians were climbing the fence to get in and on anything that had wings and wheels. Eventually, everyone was seated, the atmosphere tense, and everyone on the plane held their breath as the engines fired up to life. Artem looked out the window to see the turmoil, it was madness, civilians running as whatever security was left could do nothing other than be pushed down and trampled. The plane started moving as the runway began to be clogged with people. The pilot  turned to Artem. 

"Sir, it seems that the runway is blocked, we-"

"I don't care! Just take this plane off the ground!"

The pilot looked at him in disgust but held his tongue as a gunshot broke the silence. A security enforcer was shot as people were rushing towards the plane. The pilot pushed the throttle forward. People ducking mere meters from the wing. Artem looked down, as his heart sank seeing men in black uniforms entering the airport. The ground became smaller and smaller as he finally breathed a sigh of relief. The pilot mimicked Artem.

"Systems are nominal, we will be arriving in-"

All of a sudden, a loud  beeping emitted from the dashboard of the cockpit. Before anybody could say anything, the whole plane was engulfed in a fireball. It was almost a painless death. Five thousand feet below the fireball, a Black League officer simply said on his radio while standing next to his SAM launcher.

options.name: [Change Later]"Missile, hit!"[Change Later]

title: Ashes to Ashes
desc:
At 09:00 in the morning, Black League Troops entered the city of Bratsk situated on the Angara Sea. The City was previously bypassed by League troops on their advance. Reports showed that a sizable number of anarchist resistance has been reported, in response two infantry divisions have been ordered to move in from the north and west to secure the city. At around 10:00 the first serious combat began with orders to use artillery fire. League soldiers faced almost fanatical resistance from the local militia. At 10:30 the east of the city was fully secure with low to no resistance left. The Resistance in the West had seemingly no end with resistance to its fullest. At 12:00, a tank brigade was moved into the city.

At 13:30, North and South were cut into two, resistance was finally showing signs of slowing down. Already a quarter of the city was in rouble. Anarchists were using everything they had to fight, including bricks, rocks and even ramming cars into troops. At 14:50 with the help of the tank brigade, most of the fighting in the south of the city has ceased with all attention to the north now. Casualties, while not very high, were still a reason for concern for our troops. At 16:00 fighting in occupied areas ceased as our troops finished preparing for the final push. At 16:40 After a lengthy artillery bombardment, our troops entered the last pocket of resistance. Despite the long artillery bombardment, morale seemed to have not disappeared, and the resistance fighters still fought on. At 18:00, most of the fighting has ceased. The city is in absolute ruin, most of the civilians have fled or fought over what's left. Close to no resistance fighters surrendered. It is debatable if there is any worth in rebuilding the town or if it's better off just a burning memory.

options.name: Mother Anarchy embraces her sons for the last time.

title: [Change Later]"All is Lost"[Change Later]
desc:
[Change Later]"The city was burning. The air was choked with ash and smoke and embers, scraps of a dream deferred that drifted on the wind like fireflies. Private Koslov held his left arm over his face, hoping to ward the sting from his watering eyes. He failed. The young man, barely sixteen, stumbled over wood and rubble, his kalashnikov clutched by the cold barrel.

In the distance, he could hear screaming. The invaders were growling, roaring their hate like animals. They had slipped past language into the primordial. Beneath their shouts, he could hear civilians — women — begging for mercy. Their speech was crushed under the hammerfall of gunshots.

Koslov's bowels ran cold. The stripling broke out in a sweat as he scrabbled through chalk and fallen beams, forcing himself forward on his hands and knees. He had to escape. He had to get away from this nightmare, retreat, live to fight another day -

"Help me." A phantom's moan drifted on the burning wind.  "Please... help me."

Koslov wiped the tears and smoke from his eyes. Everything around him was an indistinguishable ruin, the same pattern of broken concrete and toppled walls. Without thinking, the words slipped from his mouth. "W-where-" He cleared his throat, spitting black phlegm into the dust. "Where are you?"

A scraping sound came from his left, and Koslov saw him. He was a man, or the remnants of one. The soldier was middle aged, balding, with a curly grey beard and the patch of the Utopian salon's militia sewn onto the breast pocket of his uniform. And his legs had been crushed by a falling beam. An arm dangled by the man's side, useless.

Koslov knew what the soldier wanted before he even spoke. Mercy. A reprieve from the animals that hunted Tomsk's ruins. But the League was close, and growing closer by the second. He could feel their breath on his neck...

"I'm sorry." The boy turned as the soldier wailed in horror, and sprinted for the city's outskirts. For survival, and shame."[Change Later]

options.name: [Change Later]"Pragmatism — another word for cowardice."[Change Later]

title: All the Queen’s men
desc:
Desperation and melancholy hung thick in the air like a choking miasma, and everyone present at the small camp was fully aware of it, from the logistics staff and soldiers all the way up to Lydia herself. But, even if this would be their final hour on Earth, the least she could do for these men was to provide the illusion that it would be worthwhile. That they would achieve something, even if only minor. The cavalrymen were mounted and neatly lined up, though not half as many as she would have wanted, most of all when faced with tanks. Slowly but purposefully, she took her own mount to front and center of the line, facing the men and scanning them sternly. Some met her stony glare, others looking decidedly more glum.

She turned her steed around, saber pointed into the air, and with a battle cry charged. Even when pushing their mounts to full speed, the only thing most men there expected to achieve was a glorious death. As they made their way over a small hill which had been covering their position, the extent of the Black League attack became fearfully obvious to all. A lump rose in her throat, but there was no turning back now.

The fleet of tanks and other armored vehicles wasted no time in turning their guns towards the cavalry charge. The thump of cannons and rattle of machine guns was the death knell for many, and those not immediately killed by a bullet were thrown to the ground. Lydia was no exception. A pair of bullets slammed into her chest, flinging her to the cold, hard ground below.

Numb from the waist down as a pool of blood slowly started to spread out, her weary thoughts turned to her father, the so-called “Rurik II”. For all his eccentricities, he truly did believe that he had been building a better future for Russia. How bitter then that this dream was torn from them. Then, her brother Yuriy drifted into focus. For all their arguments and power struggles, she did in her heart of hearts love him as any family should. She didn't know his fate; perhaps that was for the best. As darkness began to claim her, her thoughts became fearful.

options.name: Light, they always said there’d be light...

title: All the King’s men
desc:
A series of distant rumbles sent a thin layer of fine dust from the ceiling, to the table around which King Yuriy and a handful of his guards sat. The situation was dire, and everyone there knew it. A large contingent of Black League infantry was about to split their defenses in the city center in half, allowing a straight shot to their command post. They were stretched to breaking point as it was, and no reinforcements or support fire could be spared. But one last desperate plan hatched in the unfortunate king’s mind. A withdrawal, and a last stand to frustrate the attackers into halting their advance for the moment.

They still had radio contact with the front line, a mere 200 meters away. The defenses were a little more solid closer to their position, and could hold at least temporarily. With a shaking hand, which he clenched to avoid showing weakness, he ordered this tactical withdrawal. The remaining forces were exhausted and low on supply, but still fought on with a gritty determination to at least take a few more attackers with them into the arms of the reaper.

Another explosion rocked the crumbling building, closer now, yielding a much larger shower of dust particles. Feverishly, Yuriy rifled through his mind as though it were a collection of documents in a filing cabinet. Strategies, tactics, options... But alas, there was nothing.

At the front of the room, coated in dust but nonetheless unmistakable, hung a large portrait of his late father, “Rurik II” he had called himself until his final moment. A lump rose in his throat, Yuriy had hoped that when his time came,  it would be peaceful and in the company of loved ones. But it was not to be. In less than an hour, this place would be overrun, there was no stopping it.

With a deep and sharp breath through his nose, he wordlessly rose to his feet, eyes still focused on the painting. A single tear rolled out of the corner of one of his eyes, which he quickly wiped away. Nobody truly chooses their end, but one must play the hand they’re dealt. He picked up a Mosin rifle from behind him, as well as a bandolier with several spare clips on it, even attaching a bayonet. Every man present armed himself, following his lead. And with one final look at his father’s visage, he exited the room, and entered history.

options.name: My Fatherland is dying.

title: Dishonorable discharge
desc:
The war was utterly lost. That much was obvious to Boris Shepunov and anyone else with eyes and ears, but the man himself was somewhat less concerned than most. His Japanese benefactors were less than pleased at the outcome of the war, especially considering just how much investment they had poured into Shepunov’s upstart statelet. But nonetheless, it appeared they still had some sort of use for him, as they had arranged to extract him and a cadre of his staff and guards by helicopter.

Of all the men in the armored cars on their way to the pre-arranged landing site, one of them seethed with unspoken contempt. Not merely for the unfortunate situation they found themselves in, but for Shepunov himself. Their so-called glorious leader was bravely fleeing,escaping the consequences of his failures. The coward! The fool! But he would not get away with his spinelessness so easily; if it would be his job to drag this pitiful excuse for a leader backwards into hell, then so be it.

Shepunov himself looked tired and haggard, his sunken bloodshot eyes indicative of many sleepless nights, and his red face betraying his acquired habit of self medicating with copious amounts of alcohol. His clothes were crumpled and askew, far from the polished portraits showing him as nothing short of perfect. Anxiety burned in him like a hot coal lodged in his chest, his hands clasped tightly together to prevent them from trembling. He was a shell of a man, as all present could tell.

Everyone there bore weapons, though only one man was prepared to make use of his in short order. Eventually, the cars slowed to a stop, parking at a small helipad in the countryside outside of the city of Chita. As they got out, a pistol was quietly cocked, and its user took position behind Shepunov. The helicopter had already landed, one of the doors sliding open to greet them. One of the Japanese staff on board motioned for them to board. At that moment, the assailant drew his weapon. Wordlessly he pulled the trigger, and with a cry of anger blew a hole in the back of Shepunov’s head.

The attacker was felled mere seconds later, but departed the world with a satisfied smirk frozen on his face.

options.name: Rewarded as deserved.

title: What comes after
desc:
Department of the army.

Memorandum for: generals of the Black League and regional governors.

Subject: The integration of lands formerly held by the White Army and the fate of Mikhail Andreevich.

General: After the capture of Chita and the final capitulation of the white army, the remaining forces have fallen into disarray either fleeing into the vast forests of Yakuita or have broken off from whatever central command is left to become little better than bandits. Participating in various raids against undefended towns not fully incorporated into our administration like the barbarians they are. Full authorization to terminate these remnants in whichever way deemed necessary has been granted by central command. To accomplish this task, regional military governors will be installed who will work towards restoring order in the newly conquered territories.

Mikhail Andreevich has been confirmed dead since the capture of Chita. His body was found buried underneath the rubble of his imperial palace which had been shelled by artillery during the capture of Chita. His corpse has been safely relocated to be burned and forgotten. A weak and useless puppet to the white army, propaganda campaigns must be enacted against Mikhail as possible. We will discredit all this talk of Mikhail being a legitimate candidate with a campaign targeting the backwardness of the Russian monarchy that brought Russia to ruin in the first world war. We will also bring up Mikhail's pathetic character and his upbringing in the United Kingdom to showcase that he was a foreigner who didn't understand the needs of any Russian that lived under his banner.

With the annexation of the White Army's territory, we can now finally begin truly preparing ourselves for the Great Trail, Russia marches on, the chains that the white army wanted to strangle Russia with by bounding her to the past have been destroyed and the Teutons and any other country that has contributed to the destruction of Russia will feel the full might of our wrath.

options.name: Signed, Glavkoverkh Dmitry Yazov.

title: For what is it worth
desc:
Artillery fire, Planes flying, tanks rolling, ships sailing, civilians panicking, it was over. Black League Troops entered Magadan, and whatever authority the government held was gone, as is hope. The remaining politicians or troops sailed on ships on a course towards America even before the league was on the outskirts of the city, but now, without even a miracle to save it. Whatever was left, left Magadan. Petlin stayed, He didn't have anywhere, Magadan was everything he had, and now it's gone. He decided to visit an old friend. Matkovsky, as he entered the prison, it was empty, no one at the reception, no one guarding, not even a single person in a cell. Petlin entered the guard locker room, just to see one of the guards frantically packing, however after seeing Petlin he stood up straight immediately. Yet Petlin simply told him to pack up his things and see if any ships were still leaving and asked him for his keys.

Eventually, Petlin found Matovsky's cell. As he opened it Matovsky asked.

"Is my sentence up yet?" While grinning and lying on his bed. Petlin sat on a chair in his cell.

They both talked for hours, about life, their history, their families, their "friendship". Sometimes they argued, sometimes they grieved. Eventually, they ran out of things to talk about. All of a sudden artillery was heard outside as the dust off the ceiling was falling off and the lights began to dim. Petlin then took out his pistol with two bullets knowing that it was time.

Matovsky didn't react and grinned while asking.

"Was it all worth it? You and your ideas and this state you created?

Petlin didn't respond and shot him between his forehead as his corpse fell to his bed. Then he pointed his gun at his forehead and while watching Matovsky's lifeless body, he grinned and before pulling the trigger he said.

options.name: [Change Later]"Yes, yes it was."[Change Later]

title: Blood on the Snow
desc:
Matkovsky sat cold and alone in the presidential chamber, the situation was beyond dire and everyone, most of all he, knew it all too clearly. Magadan’s armies were shattered, in broken disorderly retreats and routs all across the board. Only a single understrength and poorly equipped division along with whatever militia could be scrambled stood to defend the city. They may last a little while if they’re lucky, but in the end, only death or captivity awaited them.

As for him? A protracted humiliation and torture was likely. He had read reports of what the Black League had done to other leaders, making examples of them to bring the populace to heel. Now he was directly in that firing line, potentially literally. After considering this carefully, he opened a drawer in his desk. One he had never hoped to open. It contained only a small glass bottle with a pair of white pills in it, and a flask of vodka.

While staring vacantly at the items, he drew a deep and haggard sigh, and began to reminisce about his time in Harbin, as one of the so-called “Harbin Three” along with Rodzaevsky and Shepunov as the different branches of the Russian Fascist Party. But, their desires for different types of fascism or even monarchism resulted in what was once a united effort to put the far right in control of Russia falling at the first hurdle, and splintering into a trio of statelets. It had all seemed too simple at the beginning, and he’d convinced himself that maybe, just maybe they could pull off an audacious takeover and stay together. How woefully naive, in retrospect.

He tipped the pills onto the desk and unscrewed the cap on the flask, but hesitated still. His life began to flash before his eyes, memories flooding back in a torrent of fear and nostalgia. After securing their foothold by pushing Yagoda’s reds back to Irkutsk, everyone took that opportunity to sharpen their knives. The cracks which had been slowly forming, all burst open at once. Amur, Transbaikal and Magadan were the result of this. Nobody won, not really. Even after his erstwhile peers were conquered and subsumed, it felt like a hollow victory. Symbolic at most.

He picked the pills up, placing them on his tongue before sending them down with a generous swig of vodka. The Black League would be denied their prize. This is the way the war had left him. No hope, no love, no glory, no happy ending.

options.name: He died choking, like a dog.

title: Rust
desc:
Svetlana Stalina lazily gazed at the room before her. Damp, worn, and decaying, it cast comfort from its domain and banished tranquility further still. She looked upon the men and women crowded in the holding cell with her. Once, they had made fiery speeches to their foes in the open, and to their allies behind closed doors. Now, they sat lifeless. Damp, worn, and decaying, molded by the tyrant king whose walls they slumped against.

It was the last room they would ever see.

"Number 8452!"

She stood up as two authoritative hands clasped her shoulders, and led her between her fellow prisoners, miring in the sullen stares of the people she had failed. Where had it all gone wrong? She had forsaken everything to build a Russia worth living in: her time, her health, even her morals. She had looked on as the light of democracy dimmed, and turned away, content in the fact that it was all for the people, all for Russia. Now, the light had been snuffed out, its candle nothing more than a damp, worn, and decaying obituary.

The blindfold was wet and heavy. She would never see her native land again. She didn't want to. She had been warned. God, she had been warned that those who sold democracy for security got neither. And she had pushed them away like the naive fools they appeared to be. But they were right. An insidious evil, one then basked in its malign despotism, had exploited her failings, turned her army into dust, turned her own people against her. They had won. The room she now sat in was a testament to it.

"READY!"

Could she have done things differently? Altered Russia's very destiny? Maybe. But perhaps her people had suffered too much. Perhaps there was nothing anyone could do to escape their fates. Perhaps the world really did need to bathe in hatred and hellfire if anything were to truly change. Such questions had plagued her mind since she could at last remember, demanding answers, but never receiving them.

"FIRE!"

But, at the very least, she would worry no longer.

options.name: Bullets pierce. Steel shatters.

title: What's left?
desc:
The winds blowing on the fields with overgrown grass, the sun between the mountain range's peaks, and the suspiciously peaceful and silent environment of the Siberian Taiga made him uneasy. For weeks they hid, in ruins, forests, the mountains, and in cellars, avoiding League patrols. They had no plan, no organization, perhaps no tomorrow. They had been following a creek the past few days until they were forced to flee into the mountains to avoid the League airforce. They needed someplace to rest, to reorganize, to think. Finally, after what seemed forever, the group leader turned around and told them to rest. He placed down a blanket on which they placed their remaining ammunition, rations, and grenades. He took a deep breath and looked down the valley. It was quiet. It made him even more paranoid. He thought of the day he left home. He thought of the day of his oath. He thought of the day they received the news.

The Leader inspected the blanket thoroughly while muttering under his breath. He turned his head up and asked, "That's it?" Another soldier reached into his pocket and pulled out about 5 or 6 more bullets and uncomfortably said he forgot. The Leader cursed the soldier under his breath. Eventually, he lifted his head, breathed a heavy sigh, and lifted his cap to scratch his forehead.

"Should last us a couple of weeks until we decide what to do. Hopefully, we aren't detected; a single major attack would deplete this."

Before the Leader could finish his sentence, the group was interrupted by the sound of rumbling. Just down the valley, a lonesome tank was passing by on a dirt track. The whole group ducked down. He clenched his rifle hard, not moving a muscle. Each breath became more heavy than the one before. One of the soldiers picked up a grenade and a mag and slowly began moving forward, but the Leader quickly stopped him by pulling his belt. The Leader slapped the back of his head but spared the scolding for another time. From what seemed like an eternity the group slowly emerged as they peeked over the overgrown grass. But he did not. He was still clinging to his rifle as he lay in the dirt; repeating to himself over and over again the words.

options.name: [Change Later]"We've had a good run".[Change Later]
OMS_manchurian_skirmish.1.a
OMS_manchurian_skirmish.3.a
OMS_manchurian_skirmish.4.a

title: A True War Economy
desc:
The snow gathered on the ice that used to be a river, as the wind blew hard into his face. Watching such a trivial thing as snow was about all that remained for entertainment anymore, as the realization of just how far Komi had fallen in recent years hit him.

Krylov could only watch as the League extended its ever tightening grip over Russia, and then began to suck the joys of life out of every Russian underneath its flag. First, it was the simple things; Silverware, “Unnecessary Furniture”, and then the home appliances. Soon, the boardgames, paper, and even clothing that was considered to be “extra” were confiscated by those soldiers in the pitch-black uniforms.

Sadly, it didn’t end there. Eventually, Krylov could do nothing as he was forced out of his home and assigned to an arms plant down the road. His former housing, although not of the highest caliber in Russia, had been replaced by a single bunk bed crammed into a room only 12 feet wide.

Another tear fell down his cheek, with vivid memories of the anger and sadness of it all being displayed in his mind. He had watched as the League tore down one of Russia’s brightest beacons, and replaced it with a factory of despair and anguish. And the propaganda? It was laughable, a pitiful attempt at justifying the drainage of the Russian soul in the pursuit of vengeance.

Krylov began to pull his thinly layered coat over as much of his body as he could, with the wind picking up further, and the elegant dance of the snow transforming into a blizzard. It mattered little anyway, as the whistles of the guardsmen signaled that his break for the day was over. He turned away from the river, leaving behind the memories of what once was, and lost hope for a better tomorrow.

options.name: The last breaths of Russian freedom draw ever closer.

title: Anja
desc:
[Change Later]"Peter, eat your vegetables." Anja tried to put as much calm into her voice as possible when instructing her child. It was the only thing she could do to try and soothe his anxieties in these trying times.

Anja and her family had come during the migration in the wake of Generalplan Ost. The Reich had promised her everything, and for a time they received everything. The spoils of Russia came to her doorstep every day. The natives, turned to servants and nannies, kneeled and kissed her feet at the offer of employment, and the luxuries offered to her and her family from the land nigh limitless. But, as her sons dutifully informed her even through the censorship and black ink, they were coming.

The Slav had never been a threat to Germany. According to the most intelligent minds in all of Germany, they were subhumans and henceforth incapable of standing up against the Aryan race. Her sons were of said stock, born and bred from a line of pure-Prussian vintage going back to the times of Bismark. Yet, she could detect their desperation in every letter, every stroke of a pen which continuously decreased in quality. Neat cursive turned to hasty print and hasty print turned to panicked scrawls, nigh animalistic. And the sirens. The wretched sirens. They blared at seemingly random times in the day, forewarning of attacks that came mercilessly despite the best efforts of the city's air defense. She was told all was well. For the first time though, Anja did not believe them. As if glass was shattering on the ground, her trust in the Reich was broken.

"Mommy? Why can't we have more? I'm still hungry." Anja's thoughts went back to reality, as she saw that Peter had finished his plate. It was licked clean, pristine as if she had just washed it.

"It's because the Reich needs to give everything it can to your brave brothers and fathers, fighting the Black League, so we can be safe."

She put on a smile and stroked his hair.

options.name: The Black League moves onwards!

title: A Culture of Pillage
desc:
One small flask of water. A pack of hardtack. Some strange dried meat. That seemed to be all that this deceased German soldier had to offer him. Alexei unceremoniously threw the cadaver to the ground — as befitting the treatment of the hated enemy. Pocketing the mediocre rations, Alexei flung his gun over his shoulder and went onto the next body.

The troops had been informed roughly two weeks into deployment that they would not, in fact, be receiving any more rations from the government throughout their time in the military. They were given the directive to instead "steal from those who stole from their land" — "them" obviously being the Germans. This was met with mixed reactions. Of course, they didn't stay mixed for long, as anyone who protested was immediately shot, with their rations being distributed amongst the loyal soldiers.

Alexei didn't take to the marauding lifestyle as some of his fellow troops did. Many would group together and hide in devastated buildings, jumping out at passerby Germans like a pack of Hyenas, shooting them dead and looting their corpses.

Alexei was more of a vulture, himself. He scavenged battlefields for food that was edible. Sometimes he would take their uniform if his own got too frayed. The stench of death was his constant companion, and he honestly? He was fine with it. As far as he was concerned, this was only a fraction of the suffering the hateful teutons had inflicted on his people. He was just. Kneeling down towards the next corpse, he began to pick through his belongings. Hopefully this would be more bountiful.

options.name: Hopefully not more Hardtack.

title: Only a Matter of Time
desc:
To steady his nerves, Yazov poured another drink. For hours, he had sat alone in an office, pouring over the mountain of reports from the mobilising army on the border that piled up in front of him. His only company was an overflowing ashtray, a plate of half-eaten buterbrod and the slender bottle of vodka that stared at him as he read. Quickly taking another gulp from his glass, Yazov felt his stomach writhe like a mass of worms. He finished the glass and slammed it down as an unshakable anxiety wrapped its hands around his throat. Everything he had read, absolutely everything, was good.

It wasn’t merely good, Yazov reflected as he laid back in his chair. It was superb. Across the vast front, from the icy forests in the north to the sweltering steppe of the south, the Russian eagle screamed in fury, as its vengeful wings prepared to cover the west in perfect darkness. Russian tanks were ready to tear through the Germans’ feeble soldiers, greedily crushing any resistance under their hungry treads. Once-dreaded German bombers would be sent howling towards the earth by Russian falcons, erupting in fiery blossoms of red and gold. Even around the corrupted heart of Moskau, the Russian army would run like clockwork as the Germans’ defences were pathetic and unprepared. Everything was in place, Yazov thought as he watched it in his mind’s eye. So why did he feel so damn nervous?

He glanced at the clock. 02:37. Maybe he was just getting delirious. Sleep would cure him of this nervousness, he knew. But even as he got to his feet, the papers in front of him screamed out, as if they still had some secret he had missed. Groaning, Yazov collapsed back into the seat. He knew he wouldn’t be able to sleep without sifting through these infernal reports again.

As he continued reading, he caught himself thinking about Karbyshev. Nothing the man had told him when they knew each other, but instead the stories from the war that had made him a legend. All those years he had been held in that camp, he had inspired even the most pathetic creatures to resistance against the Germans. Karbyshev had been utterly convinced, that one day, the unstoppable German war machine would falter, and he and his comrades could rise in rebellion and free themselves. Even as Kiev, Leningrad and Moscow had fallen, he remained adamant. For a fleeting moment, Yazov realised it was only a matter of time before the clockwork snapped.

Angrily, he stood, clenching the paper between strong, short fingers. Karbyshev’s day had never come, he told himself, nor would the Germans’. Karbyshev’s faith had not saved him, nor would the Germans’. Everyone Karbyshev had ever known was murdered.

options.name: So would the Germans.

title: Never Waste a Good Crisis
desc:
Watching thin fingers of steam rise from a cup of tea, Yazov waited in silence. All morning, he’d done nothing but listen to reports from the front, of failure after failure. There didn’t seem to be a clear reason for these failures; the long-awaited breakthrough had simply never come. The army was hardly unprepared, Yazov thought to himself, and the Germans shouldn’t have been able to put up such a defence. Anger curled in Yazov’s stomach like a dragon as he hunted for traitors in his mind. If the treachery wasn’t on the frontlines, it must be festering inside his own government.

“Comrade Glavkoverkh,” Sakharovsky muttered as he slid into the room, clutching a stack of files, “You’ve heard the reports from the front?”

Yazov nodded slowly, taking a sip of tea.

“We’ve compiled a number of responses here,” Sakharovsky gestured to the tower of paper that he had placed on the table, “For your selection, of course.”

“That won’t be necessary, Alexander Mikhailovich.”

“No?”

“No,” Yazov repeated firmly, “Continue executing the plan as is.”

“With respect, the current plan is failing.”

“There’s still time,” Yazov invited Sakharovsky to sit, “It’s a question of willpower. The Germans are putting up everything they have in the hopes it will send us scurrying back behind the Urals. I won’t be the first to blink.”

“Dmitry Timofeyevich,” Sakharovsky poured himself a cup of tea, “Perhaps a different approach should be considered.”

Yazov sat quietly, looking back at Sakharovsky curiously. Perhaps in an attempt to dodge the Glavkoverkh’s cold stare, Sakharovsky looked down into the depths of his tea, slowly mixing in a cube of white sugar. For the longest minute, the only sound in the room was the delicate ring of a spoon on the side of the teacup.

“How long have we prepared for this, Alexander Mikhailovich? How many years? Only to stumble at the first hurdle?”

A moment.

“No.”

“No,” Yazov nodded, “The Great Trial cannot be stopped. We do, however, have traitors in our midst. This is an internal affair.”

“Internal? Lazarenko has a talent for fear. I’d recommend him.”

“Not Lazarenko,” Yazov grimaced, “He’s too... loud. I want this done quietly.”

“Quietly,” Sakharovsky nodded, “No blood on the streets?”

“No blood, only whispers. Just enough to keep people looking over their shoulders, and doing everything they can for their Motherland.”

“Understood,” Sakharovsky rose from his seat, gathering his files, “Although a little blood may need to be spilled.”

Yazov sighed and leaned back into his chair, as Sakharovksy left. Alone, his mind wandered. Before he could stop it, a flame of doubt flickered. To dispel it, Yazov muttered to himself quietly as he rose from his chair.

options.name: “The Great Trial cannot be stopped. Never.”

title: Hold the Line
desc:
[Change Later]"Ach! Schise!" Kurt bashed the side of his MG with his palm, desperately trying to fix the feed jam. He worked frantically, every few moments glancing out of his dugout for Russian troops. He wasn't sure how long was left until the next onslaught, but it couldn't be enough.

Russia and the Black League... Kurt had never seen anything like them. He was only eighteen, but he remembered the famines and death of the Burgerkrieg as a young boy. It may have been hard but the front was... the stench of the bodies, the smell of the gas never leaving his lungs... These were animals. The Black League had charged his trench line three times. He could make out nothing but black uniforms and the stench of chlorine. They charged again and again, achieving nothing but spilling their own blood. Kurt couldn't stop staring out of the MG nest at the corpses. He went to wretch but the month old rations held in his stomach.

His empty gaze was interrupted by something breaking through the line. His eyes widened and he scrambled to battle position. They were back. He gave one last hopeless bash to the machine gun, glancing between the ever advancing charge and the weapon, and was shocked to see it cycle a round. He threw his whole weight into lifting the gun onto its position and screamed as he held down the trigger, shutting his eyes and praying that the screams would stop. He could feel the bodies hit the earth as his finger dug into the metal, holding it down with all the strength he could muster. He dared to open his eyes, the wave of gas slowly beginning to subside, but the charge hadn't abated. They were getting closer. His comms were slowly filled with more and more screams. Kurt's aim became less focused as he desperately tried to gun down whoever was closest to him. Suddenly the stream of bullets stopped.

Not now. Please not now. He slammed the gun into the wall but the jam wouldn't clear, the onslaught drawing ever nearer, only meters away. He pulled the trigger and pulled it again but the gun was done for. He pulled his pistol from its holster and tried to lift his arm.

Before the pistol had left his waist he felt the air escape his lungs as a bayonet pierced his chest. He was thrown to the floor, blood and chemicals filling his mouth as he screamed a hysterical gurgle.

options.name: The black flood breaks Europe's last line.

title: Whatever it takes
desc:
“Hey Andrey, put that cigarette out. I’ve got explosives here, genius.”

“Cool it, gramps,” Andrey took a pull. “What do you want me to do? Take a break?”

“Wait,” Damir suggested. “Like the rest of us.”

“You might be able to go fourteen hours without a smoke,” Andrey replied. “And if Daniil hasn’t set anything off with his sparks over there, no-one will.”

Damir snorted. Andrey was almost right, he knew, but he couldn’t abide the younger man’s recklessness.

When the Black League had arrived in Kazan, nothing had changed for Damir. Bullets and shells tended to stay the same, regardless of ideology, he quickly noticed. Somebody always wanted to kill somebody else, and so nobodies like Damir kept their job slaving away at the production line. But as the army had become hungrier and hungrier, quality had started to slip. Soon enough, modern power tools, safety regulations and even decent steel were nowhere to be found across western Russia. Worst of all were the production quotas, increasing endlessly with no signs of slowing down. If Damir and his colleagues had any hope of meeting them, they had to juggle dozens of deadly tasks at once to create something that didn’t even deserve to be called a shell.

As Andrey stood across from him, twirling a drill while smoking that damned cigarette, Damir packed the shells. His leathery old hands worked swiftly, as they had a thousand times before. Damir would have liked to work slower, but before he had even finished a single shell, the ancient conveyor belt groaned and pulled another into view. His back ached abominably as he reached down and up and down again, filling his hands with explosives, but he did his best to ignore the pain. If he lost his rhythm, he would not be able to keep up.

After his fingers stumbled for a brief instant, he quickly tried to correct the mistake. Although his fingers knew what to do, and moved in swift, decisive strokes, his heart panicked. As he heard the conveyor belt grind into motion once more, he hurried alongside it, desperately trying to fix his error. He tried to scream out to Andrey, to tell him to get down behind something, but there wasn’t enough time. Before Damir could even open his mouth, he felt himself swirling into the whirlpool of the pale blue sky.

options.name: I hope he enjoyed that cigarette.

title: No Dissident
desc:
Tyumen City Police Report A/11 

Status of Anti-Trial Dissidents

We are pleased to report that all districts of Tyumen are henceforth clear from all anti-Trial dissidents, without regard for age or ideology. Although the battle was tough, the brave officers of Tyumen have carried out their duties without fault. For promotion and commendation, I could recommend nobody more qualified than Sergeant Pavlov Dmitrovich who showed exemplary bravery in combatting armed anti-Trial cells in downtown Tyumen.

As the battle against anti-Trial forces was escalating to unseen levels, Sergeant Pavlov Dmitrovich took executive action against subordinates which he considered incompetent. He immediately excised all anti-Trial thought and speech from the units under his command and went onto lead them in both investigative and combative situations without regard for his own safety or the safety of his officers against those who expose themselves traitors to the state. Without loss, he successfully defeated a cell of well over three dozen fighters. In addition, he (again without loss) successfully intercepted and eliminated several illegal hubs of propaganda production and distribution.

Without the contributions of brave men such as Sergeant Dmitrovich, it cannot be said for certain that our victory would be so complete. However, with the brave efforts of all officers in the Tyumen Secret Police, I am pleased to report total and undeniable victory against anti-trial forces. Dissent has been rendered untenable for our great mission against the hated enemy.

Yours truly, 

Captain Rytin Vissarion Vitalievich

options.name: Nowhere left to run.

title: No Death is Meaningless
desc:
Beneath his feet, the concrete seemed to shift like a thrashing dog. A black mist clung to the towering silhouettes of buildings beside him, blotting the sun from the sky. Sasha could barely see out of the gas mask as it were, but the dark fog had made him nearly blind. A ferocious roar echoed from the street beside him, and when he turned he saw the black figures of his comrades charging forwards, gunfire crackling from their shadowy fingertips. In an instant, their warcry was drowned out by the thundering wail of artillery, beating the earth beneath him like a drum. When Sasha desperately ran forwards, it felt like he was falling. Between his frostbitten fingers, Sasha clung to his rifle like a Bible, tight against his chest. He tried calling out to his comrades, but his voice was drowned out in the sea of war. 

Sasha’s division was the sixth to have attacked this position. The other five had failed, and so it was up to Sasha and his comrades to prove their redemption by blood. On the first day of their attack, they encountered no resistance and took it as an easy victory. It only took one day to prove them wrong. The German dogs had blocked off streets to funnel them into a tight pocket, before gunning them down in narrow chokepoints. As Sasha’s comrades tried to force their way out, hell had opened from above their heads, in a storm of rockets and bombs. When noxious gasses had come raining from the sky too, Sasha had quickly strapped his gas mask on, and he had not seen clearly since. 

Other men might have collapsed after days like this, but not Sasha. Even as he blindly groped his way through the collapsing streets, hate burned hot inside him. Not for the enemy, but for the League. He had given them everything he had that they had asked for. Every drop of sweat and scrap of skin. But now, they thrust a rifle in his hand and tell him to die for them? When the order had been given, the officer giving it had stared at them with disgust and said, “The price of redemption is blood.” 

Sasha fell in line with his comrades, emerging ghostlike out of the fog. His feet matched their rhythm as they delved forward. Sasha found himself charging, filled with anger again. He had decided to live, and to kill those Black League bastards another day.

options.name: Another day never came.

title: No Wreckers
desc:
“It had been quite the weekend, as several Buryat laborers had holed themselves up inside an ammunition factory near Lake Baikal. They used whatever table, chair, or furniture they could find to keep the black league at bay. Despite Yazov's victory in the Far East, some of the locals of Buryatia still clung to the ideals that Sablin had given them. Ideals that kept the strikers fed and well-supplied via sympathizers within the area. As such, they refused to negotiate with the local police force.

"Workers of Buryatia unite! Unite for free and fair labor!" The young Buryat activists rallied the workers who supported them as they tried to keep up morale and make the local government concede to their demands. Chief of which was the shortening of working hours and working days. But alas, the great trial had no time nor patience for 'complainers,' and neither did Yazov or his men.

In the dead of night, a Black League battalion arrived on the factory's grounds and began burning the barricades the strikers had set up. The soldiers soon shot anyone present in the area dead, whether they had been part of the strike or not. When the soldiers had finished off the strikers, they soon moved into the villages surrounding the factory. Anyone who they suspected of harboring Sablinist ideals was quickly rounded up and driven to the remote wilderness nearby, where they were burned thoroughly by the flamethrower troops.

By Monday morning, the only trace that the strikers or the sympathizers were there was the black soot on the floors of the ammunition factory and the empty houses in the villages surrounding it. That, too, was wiped away as the factory's new workers cleaned up the mess, and loyal citizens of the black league occupied the empty houses. The following week, it was back to routine, with all who witnessed The Black League's fury being silent, lest it be them next.”

options.name: No excuses!

title: A Few Questions
desc:
A quiet, cold breeze filled the dimly lit interrogation chamber. Two earnestly dressed officers armed with revolvers sat side by side in front of a woman, a soldier of the black army. The two men look at the woman's face with cold, harsh eyes as the woman averts any eye contact with the men. She's distressed by the conversation and appears to be holding back tears.

"Once again, recruit, explain to us the incident. In detail, make sure you miss nothing."
